transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-03
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Ryan Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Malik (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Product), Alex Park (CTO, Meridian Data), Samira Khan (ML Eng), Ethan Cole (Infra), Maya Lin (PM)

Summary:
Quick walkthrough of the Model Catalog 'suitability cartography' concept — mapping open models to Meridian's vertical constraints (latency, cost, on-prem fraction), demo of Console+Optimize suggestions, and a bench plan for a 72-hour evaluation. Discussed VPC/KMS/SOC2 concerns and routing fallbacks. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics:
- Catalog filtering and model suitability scoring
- Bench run configuration (sequence length, batch size, quantization variants)
- Compatibility matrix and kernel mapping (GPU families)
- API routing policies and fallback variants
- Security/compliance checklist for Private deploy

Action items (recap at end): see metadata.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ryan (AE): Hi everyone, thanks for carving out the time. I think we have about an hour, maybe a bit over. I'm Ryan, I'll run the high level and Priya will jump in with the console and bench bits — Diego's on for product questions.

[00:22] Alex (CTO): Thanks Ryan. We want to focus on choosing open models that meet our latency SLAs but also keep cost reasonable, and understand what parts of this can run in our VPC. We're fairly strict about PII and audit logs.

[00:36] Priya (SE): Great, that's exactly what this 'cartography' session is for — we map the catalog to your constraints and show candidate bench configs. Quick note, the catalog has model metadata like tokenization, typical latency per sequence length, and compiled kernel compatibility across A100/V100/H100-ish families. Sometimes the transcription of kernel names in our exports gets slighly off, so I'll call out specifics.

[01:05] Samira (ML): One practical question up front — do you store any input data in Redwood hosted logs? Our legal team asks about data residency and retention.

[01:17] Ryan (AE): Short answer: for Hosted API, request payloads can be logged for service analytics but we have retention controls; for Dedicated and Private you control retention and logs live in your VPC or on prem. We'll include the SOC2 and KMS notes in the packet.

[01:40] Ethan (Infra): And SSO? We use Okta with SCIM provisioning and need RBAC.

[01:47] Diego (Product): We support SAML/SSO, SCIM, and you can bind RBAC rules per-route. For Private deployments we integrate with customer IdPs.

[02:05] Priya (SE): Okay jumping into the Console — I'm going to share my screen, callouts every few screens. (pause, screen fx noises)

[02:26] Priya (SE): Here is the catalog filter panel. On the left you add constraints: target p99 latency, max cost per 1k tokens, preferred quantization (fp16, int8, int4), and hardware families. We then rank models by a suitability score: a weighted blend of latency fit, cost-per-token, and evaluation score on your selected benchmark set. The weightings are adjustable.

[02:58] Maya (PM): That suitability score — is it deterministic or based on sampled benches?

[03:07] Priya (SE): It's hybrid — baseline perf numbers come from our verified benchmark corpus per model variant, then we simulate your traffic profile to estimate percentiles. If you run a sample bench with your prompts we update the score to be empirical.

[03:35] Alex (CTO): What about model variants? We have teams that want the most accurate model even if it's slightly slower.

[03:43] Priya (SE): We surface variants: full fp16, fused-int8, and a trimmed fast variant with smaller context window. On the compatibility matrix you'll see which variants compile to which GPU kernels. For example, a fused int8 path may map best to A100 80GB with our custom kernel; H100 may need a different kernel selection and will alter latency.

[04:10] Samira (ML): Do you provide quantization recommendations? We currently run q4f16 for some workloads.

[04:18] Priya (SE): Yes Optimize will recommend quantization profiles by workload. In the demo I have two suggested profiles for your prompt set: q4f16 for general L2 summary tasks, and int8 for high-throughput classification. We'll show expected quality delta and token-cost savings.

[04:40] Ryan (AE): Real quick on tradeoffs — higher quantization reduces cost but can regress on sensitive generative tasks; we surface evaluation deltas against holdout prompts so you can see exact examples where outputs differ.

[05:02] Priya (SE): Jumping to the bench runner: here we configure a 72-hour bench with three axes — model variant, hardware family, and batching config. We recommend starting with small batch sizes to meet latency SLO then run a few burst configs to measure throughput.

[05:30] Priya (SE): I'll load a sample plan: 10k request mix, sequence length distribution 20/80/200 tokens, and three model variants mapped across A100/H100/RTX pools. Note — the sampling engine will capture KV cache hit rates if you enable prefix caching in the runtime.

[05:55] Ethan (Infra): Prefix caching — is that something we control in Private? We want predictable memory use.

[06:03] Priya (SE): Yes, in Private you expose the cache limits and eviction policy. In Dedicated there's an autoscaled cache layer with configurable TTL.

[06:20] Alex (CTO): On the compatibility matrix — can you export that for our infra team? We need kernel mapping and suggested instance types.

[06:29] Priya (SE): Absolutely — you can export a CSV with model, variant, kernel, recommended GPU family, expected p50/p95 latency at the configured batch size, and cost estimate per 1M tokens.

[06:42] Samira (ML): A few more gotchas: how tolerant is the runtime to sequence length spikes? We sometimes get occasional 2k token queries.

[06:52] Priya (SE): The runtime prioritizes requests by policy — you can set a hard cutoff or allow fallbacks to a cheaper model variant that supports longer contexts. We also have a streaming fallback where long requests stream with lower concurrency to avoid head-of-line blocking.

[07:14] Diego (Product): Another note on routing: you can route by cost (send to cheaper variants during off-peak), by region (latency sensitive requests keep local), or by customer tier. Fallback policies are first-class.

[07:40] Ryan (AE): Okay I'm going to hand over to a quick example of an API call pattern and how you attach a rollout policy in a route.

[07:48] Ryan (AE): Example curl: POST /v1/generate with model=redwood:model-x and header x-rollout-policy: canary-10. This is of course syntactic, but the console shows the same config and you can attach conditions such as token budget or route weights.

[08:12] Maya (PM): Can we pin a specific model version for a business-critical route?

[08:18] Priya (SE): Yes pinning and versioned rollout is supported; you can do canary, A/B, or gradual rollout. The console also lets you inspect per-model token cost and regressions vs a golden prompt set.

[08:40] Alex (CTO): Security question again — if we go Private, what parts of the control plane still call Redwood? Are there callbacks?

[08:51] Ryan (AE): In Private with the full control plane in your VPC, telemetry can be routed to your logging endpoints. There's an optional control-plane egress for licensing checks but it can be minimized or audited per contract. We'll include the network diagram and egress list.

[09:10] Samira (ML): During the bench, do you run the exact containerized kernels or simulated perf? We need confidence the bench equals production.

[09:21] Priya (SE): We run the actual runtime builds on the target GPU families — the bench runner can be executed in our hosted infra or in your environment (Dedicated/Private) for apples-to-apples. For earlier POC we typically run both to identify deltas.

[09:44] Diego (Product): I'll add that we keep a kernel-compatibility table and version mapping; occasionally a vendor driver update shifts perf, so we record driver versions in bench metadata.

[10:02] Alex (CTO): Good. Pricing — is the Hosted price per token only, or are there express tiers for low-latency SLAs?

[10:10] Ryan (AE): Hosted is usage-based with optional SLA tiers for latency. Dedicated is committed capacity with a monthly attach and lower per-token. Private is enterprise licensing. We'll send a tailored pricing sheet.

[10:28] Samira (ML): Can Optimize suggest batching configs automatically? Our current heuristics are ad-hoc.

[10:35] Priya (SE): Yes Optimize will recommend batching + concurrency knobs based on your request distribution and SLO targets. It also suggests prefix caching settings to reduce token work.

[10:52] Maya (PM): Any examples of quality regressions from quantization we can review?

[10:58] Priya (SE): We have side-by-side diffs in the console; for one sample L2 summarization task with int8 we saw a small BLEU-ish drop and a few hallucination cases, we flag those. You can view exemplar prompts where outputs diverge.

[11:20] Alex (CTO): Alright this is helpful — say we pick three models to bench, run 72 hours in your hosted infra first to get baseline then mirror in our Private env. What's the timeline?

[11:32] Ryan (AE): If we get your prompt sets today, Priya can assemble a bench config and run the hosted baseline within 48–72 hours. Then we can sync to run in your Private env once we have network access — that is usually another 3–5 business days depending on infra setup.

[11:50] Ethan (Infra): For Private we'll need the helm chart or operator and some docs about required kernel drivers.

[11:58] Diego (Product): We'll send the operator manifests and a driver compatibility checklist.

[12:07] Ryan (AE): Okay, let's recap next steps — Ryan send pricing and SOW, Priya assemble bench config and run initial hosted baseline, Meridian to share prompts and token profile, Diego will attach operator docs and network egress list.

[12:20] Alex (CTO): Sounds good. Any final questions?

[12:24] Maya (PM): One last: can we get a short one-page summary of the cartography approach for our execs?

[12:30] Ryan (AE): Yes we'll draft a one-pager with the suitability score explanation, bench plan, and risks.

[12:36] Alex (CTO): Perfect. Thanks everyone.

[12:40] Ryan (AE): Thanks all, we'll follow up with the packet.

End of transcript.
